tier_reason: Peer-reviewed PVLDB 16(1) paper compares against RocksDB 6.14.6 (and LeanStore) and states the CPU (Xeon Gold 6230). The artifact repo has benchmark code (bench/, scripts/ycsb_v2, scripts/e2e_perf), but neither the paper nor the repo names the compiler, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: On YCSB, TreeLine outperforms RocksDB by 2.20x on average (geometric mean) across the 1024-byte-record point workloads, and by up to 10.95x overall. On uniformly distributed scan-heavy workloads (YCSB E) with 16 request threads it wins 2.50x (1024 B) and 2.21x (64 B), averaged across three datasets; on Zipfian scans it wins 1.88x (1024 B) and 1.74x (64 B). On Zipfian point workloads (Amazon dataset) it wins 1.62x (64 B) and 2.99x (1024 B). On uniform point workloads the average speedup over RocksDB is only 1.45x.
corrections.workload: YCSB point workloads (A, B, C, D, F) and scan-heavy workload E, run with the authors' own C++ YCSB implementation. Records are 64 bytes and 1024 bytes (8-byte keys), with Zipfian (theta 0.99) and uniform request distributions. Datasets are synthetic (20M keys), Amazon reviews (33M keys) and OpenStreetMap (23M keys). Each system gets memory for up to 33% of the dataset and 4 background threads. RocksDB 6.14.6 runs with block compression and SSTable checksums disabled. All runs on an NVMe SSD.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler is not stated in the paper or the repo. The repo README builds with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, and CMakeLists.txt sets C++17 and adds -march=native.
corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed PVLDB 16(1) (2022) paper, but no compiler is named anywhere (the repo builds Release with -march=native), which caps the tier at B. RocksDB was run with block compression and SSTable checksums disabled. Gains vary a lot by workload: uniform point workloads average only 1.45x over RocksDB, and LeanStore beats TreeLine on some 64 B Zipfian scan cases. This is prototype research code with no commits since January 2024.

notes: The numbers in the record are all in the paper but attached to the wrong conditions. 2.20x is the 1024 B point-workload average, not '16 threads, uniform'. 2.50x is the uniform YCSB E scan result, not a skewed one. 1.62x is the Zipfian 64 B point result, not a real-world-only figure. I rewrote the claim. Metadata checked out: MIT, 147 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2024-01-02, so stale is correct.

tier_reason: The project's own docs page reports HSE 1.7.0 vs RocksDB 6.6.4 on YCSB, with the CPU (Xeon E5-2690 v4), YCSB version and HSE config files stated. The YCSB harness is public as the hse-ycsb fork, but no compiler or flags are given, so these are first-party numbers short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Load phase: more than 8x RocksDB's insert throughput (986,009 vs 122,899 inserts/sec), 88% shorter load (34 vs 271 minutes), and 99.9th-percentile insert latency of 1.6 ms vs 19.5 ms. Run phase: 'up to nearly 6x' more throughput across workloads A-D (shown only in a chart). Tail latency is down up to 91% for writes and 42% for reads. Bytes written are down up to 85% and bytes read up to 64%.
corrections.workload: YCSB 0.17.0 workloads A-D (load and run phases) on a 2TB dataset of 2 billion 1,000-byte records, with 96 client threads and 2 billion operations per workload. HSE 1.7.0 used its shipped native_ycsb_abcdf load/run config files; the baseline was RocksDB 6.6.4.
corrections.caveats: First-party vendor benchmark from the HSE/Micron v1 docs (HSE 1.7.0 vs RocksDB 6.6.4, about 2020), not independently reproduced. No compiler or build flags are stated, and run-phase per-workload numbers appear only in chart images. GitHub's license API returns null, but the README and source SPDX headers declare Apache-2.0 OR MIT (bundled subprojects are under Zlib, BSD-2-Clause and MIT). The repo is not archived, but the last commit on master was 2023-08-17.

notes: Every number in the record matches the page; 'up to ~6x' is the page's 'up to nearly 6x'. I fixed the license to the dual Apache-2.0 OR MIT declared in the SPDX headers and .reuse/dep5. Stars (669), non-fork status and 'abandoned' (over 3 years since the last commit) are all correct.

tier_reason: The README and benchmark.md give first-party numbers against LevelDB v1.23 and SQLite v3.51.3 and state the CPU (i5-12450HX). The 'custom C++ chrono benchmarking suite' is not published in the repo, and the build compiler and flags are not stated, so this is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Small-payload test (10,000 keys, ~8-byte keys, ~10-byte values, memtable 10,000). New-key writes: 550,221 ops/s vs LevelDB's 188,175 (~2.9x, derived from page data) and vs SQLite individual-transaction mode's 11,222 (~49x, derived from page data). It is slower than LevelDB on everything else: updates (49,465 vs 188,215 ops/s), read hits (0.063 vs 0.0008 ms/op cold), read misses (0.001 vs 0.0004 ms/op) and range scans (6.58 vs 0.17 ms cold). It is also slower than SQLite's batched mode on writes and updates. With 1 KB values (benchmark.md) it loses to LevelDB on every operation, including new writes (45,709 vs 95,153 ops/s). With a 100k memtable, small-payload writes reach about 536k vs about 186k ops/s.
corrections.workload: Single-process microbenchmark of 10,000 keys run with an unpublished custom C++ chrono harness. Operations: new-key writes, half-key updates, read hits (cold and hot), read misses and range scans. Payloads are small (~8-byte keys, ~10-byte values) or 1 KB values, with memtable limits of 1k, 10k and 100k. Baselines are LevelDB v1.23 and SQLite v3.51.3 (synchronous=OFF, journal_mode=MEMORY; individual and batched transactions).
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i5-12450HX, 12GB RAM @ 4800 MT/s (single channel), 512GB NVMe SSD, Windows 11 Home 64-bit
corrections.compiler_and_flags: The benchmark build is not stated. The README build instructions name MSVC (Visual Studio 2019+) or MinGW `g++ -std=c++17 ... -lws2_32`, with no optimization flag.
corrections.caveats: Tiny single-author hobby project (3 stars). Only 10,000 keys per test, and the benchmark harness is not published in the repo. It loses to LevelDB on 4 of 5 operations with small payloads and on all 5 with 1 KB values, so the only win is small-value bulk inserts. The compiler and flags used for the benchmark are not stated, and the documented g++ build command has no -O flag. Windows-only (Winsock2). The README badge says MIT, but the LICENSE file and GitHub both say AGPL-3.0. Results are self-reported with no independent verification.

notes: Downgraded because the claim was overstated. The record said VortexDB loses 3 of 5 operations to LevelDB, but it also loses updates (3.8x slower) and read misses, and benchmark.md shows it losing even new writes with 1 KB values. The only win left is a 10k-key small-value insert test, so the orchestrator may want to treat this as marginal. Metadata checked out: AGPL-3.0, 3 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-05-27, active.
